messages.subject: Re: Distance sampling
parts:
Hi Werner,

> >1. When I select a model definition it has to be typed additionally into 2
> >other windows (in these windows there is no option of selecting models). How
> >can I be sure that the computer analyses the model first selected (then the
> >name typed somewhere else instead of being selected) and not another model?
> >During further analyses it also keeps on using the first model.

The Model Definition selected for an analysis is the one highlighted under
"Model Definition" in the Analysis Details Inputs tab. If you want to change
the name of the Model Definition you can either type in a new name there, or
click on "Properties..." and type in a new name in the Model Definition
Properties window.

I suggest you carefully read the online manual Chapter 7. This explains the
difference between an Analysis and a Model Definition, which is something people
often get confused about. Under "Working with Data Filters and Model
Definitions" it explains how to select a Model Definition for an analysis.

One of these days I'll get around to completing the getting started pages to
include an example analysis, which will hopefully make life easier for
beginners.

> >2. Why does the program forces me to ignore data collected on the line, i.e.
> >on 0 meters? Shouldn't this data be included in the analysis?

It doesn't force you to ignore this data. The default left truncation is "No
truncation" for exact data, and when you have interval data, the default lowest
cutpoint of 0 includes distances at 0. This latter point is documented in the
online manual (select the Data Filter | Intervals tab, press F1 and read the
Aside at the bottom of the page).

> >3. We surveyed 8 lines counting francolins in distance intervals. The terrain
> >did not allow for long lines. We therefore monitored 8 short lines (+- 800m
> >each), but individual lines did not produce sufficiently large numbers that
> >warrant individual analyses. We then pooled the data from the 8 lines (218
> >francolins in total). To estimate variation, should the pooled data (8 lines)
> >be bootstrapped, OR should density be estimated for each line separately and
> >then variation calculated?

I'm not sure exactly what you did here. Assuming you have each line in Distance
as a separate record in the sample layer (probably called "Line transect" in
your project), then I assume you asked in the Model Definition for a global
density estimate and global encounter rate, which is why you say you "pooled"
the data from the 8 lines. To estimate variance, use the default method, under
the Variance tab in Model definition, which is to estimate variance empirically.
How this is done is detailed in the Distance Sampling book (Introduction to
Distance Sampling pages 78-89; or you can get a copy of the previous edition
from the Distance web site). If you want to bootstrap, you can bootstrap by
sample in the Variance tab. However, 8 lines is very few for a reliable
empirical estimate of variance, and really too few for a reliable bootstrap.
For that you would ideally want at least 20-30 lines, with good spatial coverage
(see the survey design chapter in the book).

Hope this helps,

- Len
